In Haggouch, Doré-Mazars & Tagu (2026), 304 people foraged for targets of
two types (40 per trial, 20 of each) in two foraging tasks, `foraging1` and
`foraging2`, 14 trials of each. **TODO**: what the two tasks are (which
target types, and how the tasks differ). Every trial is exhaustive: people
selected all 40 targets. The paper relates foraging to executive functions
and personality; this page only models the foraging itself.

The two target types are the item classes of a categorical (`cat`) model,
and the two tasks are its conditions. With 304 people, this is by far the
largest dataset here (340,480 selections, about four times C2022), so it
estimates per-person foraging styles for a large sample: the starting
point for relating them to individual characteristics.

This page shows how to work with a fitted model: checking convergence,
reading the posterior, accuracy and posterior predictive checks. The model
is the default one: multi-level, Fourier-124
directions, the default priors, 4 chains of 1000 warmup and 1000 sampling
iterations.

*Note*: this page doesn't fit anything. It reads a saved fit
(`haggouch2026acta_fourier124.rds`) from `fits/` in this folder. It isn't
in the repository: to make it, run `fit_haggouch2026acta.R` in this folder
(about 5 hours on a laptop), which saves it there. See
`examples/real_data/README.md`.

*Note*: because the dataset is so large, the predictions and simulations
below use fewer posterior draws than the other pages (`n_pred_draws` and
`n_post_draws`, set in the first chunk). With this many selections, a few
draws already give precise accuracy and trial statistics.

Code: `haggouch2026acta.R`.

```{r}
#| include: false
knitr::read_chunk("haggouch2026acta.R")
```

## Posterior

`extract_post()` turns the fit's draws into tidy tables (one per group of
parameters), which the `plot_post_*()` functions take.

```{r extract}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr list(file.mtime("fits/haggouch2026acta_fourier124.rds"), rlang::hash(d))
```

```{r fig-post}
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Posterior densities by task: class transitions, distance and relative direction, and the Fourier coefficients. Grey bands: the priors' HPDIs."
```

The same spatial parameters, shown as what each does to an item's
selection weight:

```{r fig-post-weights}
#| fig-cap: "Relative selection weight against distance, turn and absolute direction: 53% and 97% HPDIs."
```

Each person's distance and relative-direction estimates, over the
population's. With 304 people, each row is one person, unlabelled: the
plot shows how much people vary, not who is who.

```{r fig-person}
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-cap: "Per-person estimates (intervals, one row per person) over the population-level HPDIs (grey bands)."
```

And each person's class-transition probabilities: how likely they are to
select each target type next, given the type they just selected.

```{r fig-person-cat}
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-cap: "Per-person class-transition probabilities (previous type -> next type) over the population-level HPDIs (grey bands)."
```

## Accuracy

The fit doesn't store a prediction for every selection
(`save_selections = FALSE`, the default), so `predict_fomo()` makes them
from `n_pred_draws` (50) posterior draws. Deterministic accuracy is how
often the item the model judges most likely is the one selected; the
probability of the chosen item credits being nearly right too. Chance
(dotted) is $1/n$, with $n$ the items left; the nearest-neighbour rule (dashed) always
picks the closest item, so the gap above it is what the model adds to
proximity alone. This is in-sample accuracy, which overestimates
out-of-sample accuracy.

```{r predict}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr list(file.mtime("fits/haggouch2026acta_fourier124.rds"), rlang::hash(d), n_pred_draws)
```

```{r fig-accuracy}
#| fig-cap: "Accuracy at each selection, with chance and nearest-neighbour baselines."
```

## Posterior predictive check

Whole trials simulated from the fitted model, compared with the data. The
model doesn't predict when a trial stops, so each simulated trial keeps as
many selections as the observed one (here always all 40).

```{r sim-posterior}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr list(file.mtime("fits/haggouch2026acta_fourier124.rds"), rlang::hash(d), n_post_draws)
```

```{r fig-sim-trial}
#| fig-cap: "One trial per task, simulated from the fitted model."
```

```{r fig-sim-stats}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr rlang::hash(list(found_post, trial_stats))
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Trial statistics for the data (x) and simulated from the posterior (y). Points near the diagonal mean the model reproduces them."
```
